title: How Your Gut Microbiome Controls Your Brain

slides.heading: Your Gut Controls Your Brain
slides.body: The trillions of microbes living in your digestive system are shaping your mood, memory, and mental health

slides.heading: You Are Mostly Microbes
slides.body: Your gut hosts roughly 38 trillion bacteria — outnumbering your own cells. These microbes collectively weigh about 1.5 kg and contain 150 times more unique genes than your own DNA.

slides.heading: The Gut-Brain Axis
slides.body: Your gut and brain are in constant two-way communication via the vagus nerve, immune signals, and hormones. This 'gut-brain axis' lets your microbiome directly influence how you think and feel.

slides.heading: Your Second Brain
slides.body: The enteric nervous system — a network of 500 million neurons lining your gut — operates independently of the brain. It can sense, process, and respond to information without input from your head.

slides.heading: Microbes Make Your Mood
slides.body: About 95% of your body's serotonin is produced in the gut, not the brain. Gut bacteria regulate this production, directly influencing feelings of happiness, anxiety, and overall emotional balance.

slides.heading: The Anxiety Connection
slides.body: Studies show that germ-free mice raised without gut bacteria display higher anxiety and stress. When human microbiomes are transplanted into them, they begin to exhibit the donor's behavioral traits.

slides.heading: Diet Rewires Your Mind
slides.body: A diverse, fiber-rich diet feeds beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids — compounds that reduce brain inflammation, support memory, and protect against neurodegenerative diseases.

slides.heading: Disruption Has Real Costs
slides.body: Antibiotics, ultra-processed foods, and chronic stress wipe out microbial diversity. This dysbiosis is now linked to higher rates of depression, cognitive decline, and even conditions like Parkinson's disease.

slides.heading: Probiotics as Mental Medicine
slides.body: Emerging research on 'psychobiotics' — beneficial bacteria that improve mental health — shows promise for treating depression and anxiety. Clinical trials are already testing targeted probiotic therapies.

slides.heading: Feed Your Mind from the Inside Out
slides.body: The microbiome is a frontier of medicine redefining what it means to be mentally healthy. Eat diverse whole foods, limit antibiotics, and remember: a happy gut may be the key to a healthy mind.
